title: Richest Route Across Two Sorted Tracks
statement:
Two strictly increasing arrays a and b are two tracks. You start at the first element of either track and walk left to right, collecting every value you step on.

Whenever you stand on a value that appears in both tracks, you may jump to the same value on the other track and continue from there. A shared value is collected only once.

Return the largest total you can collect by the time you walk off the end of a track, modulo 1 000 000 007. Compare totals by their real size; take the modulo only of the final answer.

examples.why: Start on b for 2, pass the shared 4, take 6 on a, pass the shared 9, finish on b with 10: 2 + 4 + 6 + 9 + 10. Better than either track alone (20 and 30).
No shared values, so you stay on one track. a sums to 6, b to 4.
Up to the 5, b offers 1 + 2 + 3 while a offers nothing. After that the tracks are identical.

hints: Shared values split both tracks into matching segments. Between two shared values, what is your choice?
Between consecutive shared values you are on one track or the other for the whole stretch, and the choice does not affect any later segment.
Walk both arrays with two pointers, summing each track's current segment. At a shared value, add the larger segment sum plus the shared value, then reset both sums. Add the larger tail at the end.

explain.intuition:
The only places where the two tracks connect are the shared values. So a route is a sequence of independent choices: for each stretch between two shared values (and before the first and after the last), take track a's stretch or track b's. Each shared value is collected no matter what.

Because the choices do not affect each other, take the larger stretch every time. Two pointers walk the sorted arrays like a merge, keeping a running sum per track; when they meet on a shared value, settle the stretch.
steps: While both pointers are in range: if a[i] < b[j] add a[i] to sa and move i; if greater, add b[j] to sb and move j.
If equal, add max(sa, sb) + a[i] to total, reset both sums, and move both pointers.
Add any leftover elements to their sums, then add max(sa, sb) to total.
pitfalls: Taking the modulo of the running sums before comparing them. A reduced sum can look smaller than it really is.
Counting a shared value twice, once on each track.
Forgetting the tail after the last shared value, or the segment before the first one.

solutions.title: Try every switch decision
solutions.idea: Recursively walk a track; at each shared value, try both staying and switching.
solutions.time: O(2^k · (n + m)) for k shared values

solutions.title: Two pointers with segment sums
solutions.idea: Sum each track between shared values and keep the larger stretch each time.

followups: There are k tracks instead of two, still sorted, and you may jump between any tracks at a shared value. How does the merge change?
Return the route itself, not just the total.
